item.title: Bedside ECMO Cannulation by Intensivists and Emergency Physicians
item.description:
The number of centers capable of initiating extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for critically ill patients with refractory cardiac or respiratory failure is expanding. Historically, patients were taken to the operating room or catheterization laboratory for ECMO cannulation by cardiothoracic surgeons and perfusionists. More recently, non-surgeons who have undergone specialized training are performing percutaneous ECMO cannulation and initiation of support at the bedside at some centers. This approach is attractive, in part, because of the timely initiation of ECMO and avoidance of the risk of patient deterioration during transport to a procedural area. The purpose of this article is to provide a roadmap for intensivists and emergency physicians to lead ECMO bedside procedures including veno-venous (VV), veno-arterial (VA), and hybrid veno-arteriovenous (V-AV) cannulation at ECMO-capable centers. These procedures demand cognitive and technical skills that are already foundational to critical care practice, including vascular access guided by point-of-care ultrasound and leadership during a dynamic resuscitation. A team-based approach to bedside ECMO cannulation is presented and illustrated with figures and video, including preparation, procedural execution, subsequent patient management, and programmatic considerations such as training and credentialing requirements.

Sheehan J, Hansen SJ, Heather B, Erickson H, Simpson NS, Robinson AE

item.title: Liberation from Veno-venous Extracorporeal Life Support (VV-ECLS) for Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): the Liberate VV-ECLS study: an international survey
item.description:
Background: The use of veno-venous extracorporeal life support (VV-ECLS) for severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) has increased substantially worldwide. However, approaches to liberation from extracorporeal support remain poorly defined, with no standardized protocols or validated readiness criteria.

Research question: What are the global practices for VV-ECLS liberation among Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) centers? Where is there variability in readiness assessment, liberation strategies, and use of standardized protocols?

Study design and methods: We formulated a cross-sectional survey of 25 questions regarding liberation practices among ECLS providers. Questions focused on assessed parameters for readiness to liberate, determination of liberation success, and strategies to optimize it. Surveys were distributed electronically to 765 institutions globally registered with ELSO between July 1st and Aug 15th, 2022. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize responses.

Results: Of 765 centers contacted, 340 (44%) responded, with 209 (61%) reporting use of VV-ECLS. Most centers were adult-focused, intensivist-led programs with moderate annual volumes. Most respondents (58%) prioritized VV-ECLS liberation before liberation from mechanical ventilation. Readiness for liberation was most determined by improvement in oxygenation under lung-protective ventilation (92%) and respiratory system compliance (90%), while fewer centers used inspiratory effort indices (34%). Liberation strategies were heterogeneous, with progressive reduction of sweep gas flow being most common (40%). Liberation trial duration varied widely (median 120 minutes; mean 497 ± 635 minutes), and most centers performed one trial per day. Arterial blood gas abnormalities (90%) and clinical signs of respiratory distress were the primary indicators of liberation failure. Only 42% of centers reported using a formal liberation protocol.

Interpretation: VV-ECLS liberation practices vary substantially across centers and are largely guided by institutional experience rather than standardized evidence. These findings highlight the need for validated physiologic predictors and protocolized strategies to optimize safe and timely liberation from VV-ECLS.

Al-Fares A, Al-Rashed M, Al-Mumin A, Del Sorbo L, Fan E

item.title: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk prediction in individuals with and without impaired spirometry
item.description:
Background: Cardiovascular disease risk scores likely underestimate risk in individuals with impaired spirometry (airflow obstruction and preserved ratio impaired spirometry (PRISm)).

Research question: How do risk scores perform between individuals with impaired and normal spirometry, and can they be improved by adding spirometry and dyspnea?

Study design and methods: Ten-year incidence of major cardiovascular events (MACE) ie., myocardial infarction, stroke or death from coronary heart disease, from 7 US population-based cohorts was used for this analysis. The pooled cohorts' equations' (PCE) ability to predict MACE was compared between normal and impaired spirometry. Cox-models adding spirometry, dyspnea to PCE variables were evaluated for improvement in MACE prediction.

Results: Among 26523 participants, those with impaired (N=7547) compared with normal (N=18932) spirometry had a higher incidence of MACE (14% vs 7%), hazard ratio 95%CI 1.25[1.17,1.34] adjusted for PCE variables. Discrimination using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC)95%CI of the PCE for MACE was 0.792[0.780,0.803] vs 0.740[0.724,0.755] in normal vs impaired spirometry. Discrimination of MACE improved slightly by adding to the PCE: dyspnea plus 1)impaired spirometry 0.792[0.783,0.800], 2)PRISm, mild, moderate+ airflow obstruction 0.792[0.783,0.801], 3)FEV1%predicted, FEV1/FVC splines 0.793[0.784,0.802], compared with PCE variables 0.790[0.781,0.798]. The differences in AUC[95%CI] were: 1)0.002[0.001,0.003]p=0.002, 2)0.002[0.001,0.004]p=0.002, 3)0.003[0.002,0.005]p=0.0005 respectively. Among participants with impaired spirometry, only the model that added FEV1%predicted, FEV1/FVC continuous and dyspnea to the PCE showed improvement in AUC[95%CI], 0.750[0.735,0.765] vs 0.746[0.730,0.761] for PCE variables, difference of 0.004[0.001,0.008]p=0.008. There were no differences among models in calibration, sensitivity, specificity, overall performance, and after bootstrapping 1000 samples.

Interpretation: Performance of the PCE was better among individuals with normal vs impaired spirometry, despite the latter having an excess burden of MACE. Adding spirometry and dyspnea to PCE variables showed a small statistically significant improvement in MACE prediction, which may not be meaningful clinically, so other risk factors should be considered.

Krishnan S, Oelsner E, Smith B, Balte PP, Farias R, Benedetti A

item.title: How I Do It: An Intensivist's guide to RV Failure and Right Ventricular Assist Devices
item.description:
Right ventricular failure (RVF) is a high-mortality form of cardiogenic shock frequently encountered in critical illness and is often underrecognized due to its heterogeneous presentation. This article presents a physiology-driven, stepwise approach to the diagnosis and management of acute RVF using a longitudinal case in the intensive care unit. We highlight practical bedside tools for recognition, including point-of-care ultrasound and invasive hemodynamics, and review targeted strategies for preload optimization, afterload reduction, and contractility support. Special emphasis is placed on airway management, vasoactive medications, and timely escalation to mechanical circulatory support (MCS) in appropriately selected patients. This bedside "How I Do It" guide is written for intensivists and pulmonary/critical care clinicians and translates advanced hemodynamic and device concepts into practical decision points for acute care management.

Sridhar M, Patel M, Manek G, Chowdhury J, Villalobos N, Soto F

item.title: Comparative Effectiveness of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists versus DPP-4 and SGLT2 Inhibitors in Patients with Bronchiectasis and Type 2 Diabetes
item.description:
Background: Bronchiectasis is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with limited disease-modifying therapies. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects, but their impact on bronchiectasis outcomes remains unknown.

Research question: Is GLP-1RA use, compared with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP-4i) or sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) use, associated with better clinical outcomes in patients with bronchiectasis and type 2 diabetes (T2D)?

Study design and methods: Using the TriNetX global federated research network, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with bronchiectasis and type 2 diabetes who initiated GLP-1RA therapy between June 1, 2022, and May 30, 2025. We compared clinical outcomes, including all-cause mortality, bronchiectasis exacerbation, acute respiratory failure, and lower respiratory tract infections, with patients receiving DPP-4i) or SGLT2i using propensity score matching to balance baseline characteristics.

Results: After propensity score matching, 1,029 patients per group were included in the GLP-1RA versus DPP-4i cohort, and 2,255 patients per group in the GLP-1RA versus SGLT2i cohort. Compared with DPP-4i, GLP-1RA use was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratio [HR], 0.43; 95% CI, 0.33-0.56) and reduced risks of acute respiratory failure (HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.36-0.58) and lower respiratory tract infection (HR, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.46-0.65). Similar benefits were observed compared with SGLT2i for all-cause mortality (HR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.40-0.60), acute respiratory failure (HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.39-0.55), and lower respiratory tract infection (HR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.68-0.86). Stratified analyses demonstrated consistent mortality benefits across demographic and clinical subgroups, with particularly pronounced effects in obese patients but there was no statistically significant reduction in bronchiectasis exacerbations.

Interpretation: Among patients with bronchiectasis and type 2 diabetes, GLP-1RA therapy was associated with significantly lower mortality and reduced respiratory complications compared with DPP-4i or SGLT2i. These findings suggest potential disease-modifying benefits of GLP-1RAs in bronchiectasis beyond glycemic control.

Liao KM, Chuang YM, Hsu WH, Kuo CY, Wu JY, Shiau BW

item.title: The Burden of Chronic Cough in Patients With Interstitial Lung Disease: a US Survey-Based Analysis of Its Effects on Daily Life and Emotional and Social Well-Being
item.description:
Background: Chronic cough (≥8 weeks) is highly prevalent among patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and non-IPF interstitial lung disease (ILD) and imposes significant physical, social, and psychological burden. Research characterizing the burden of chronic cough in patients with IPF and non-IPF ILD from the patient perspective is limited.

Research question: What is the multidimensional burden of chronic cough in patients living with IPF or non-IPF ILD?

Study design and methods: An online cross-sectional survey was distributed to adults from June to July 2025 via the Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation's US Community Registry. Eligibility required a self-reported diagnosis of IPF or non-IPF ILD and chronic cough. Multiple-choice and open-text questions spanned six domains: demographics, disease history, cough characteristics, daily life impact, social/emotional and long-term impact, and healthcare experience.

Results: A total of 197 participants completed the survey: 75.63% reported a diagnosis of IPF, 21.32% reported non-IPF ILD, and 3.05% were awaiting further ILD diagnosis. Participants reported cough-related interference with daily activities (76.15%) and sleep disruption (79.69%) within the preceding week. Emotional burden was frequently reported: 95.94% of participants had cough-induced worry, 75.13% had depression, sadness, or low mood, and 67.01% reported avoiding social situations because of cough. Additionally, 60.91% of participants reported that chronic cough affected their platonic relationships, and 55.33% reported impact on their ability or desire to maintain physical or intimate relationships. To treat cough, participants reported using an average of 2.7 therapeutic classes historically and 2.0 classes currently, with many reporting limited or no relief.

Interpretation: Findings from this US survey of patients with IPF or non-IPF ILD and chronic cough indicate that, among respondents, chronic cough burden manifests physically, psychologically, and psychosocially. Reports of limited relief from available therapies suggest an unmet need in managing chronic cough in this patient population.

Clinical trial registration: Not applicable.

Swigris J, Kulkarni T, Watterston C, Nakano A, Barrett K, Shore JE
